Title: Document cursor pagination for the /v2/items endpoint
Type: Documentation
Priority: Medium
Labels: docs, api, good-first-issue
Status: In Review

--- Description ---

The /v2/items endpoint switched from page numbers to cursor pagination in the
last release, but the reference page still describes the old `page` and
`per_page` parameters. Several users have asked in the discussion board how to
get the second page. We need a short how-to plus an updated parameter table.

Proposed content for the how-to:

## Paginating through items

Responses from `GET /v2/items` contain at most `limit` objects (default 50,
maximum 200). When more results exist, the response includes a `next_cursor`
string. Pass it back unchanged as the `cursor` query parameter to get the
following page. When `next_cursor` is null you have reached the end.

    GET /v2/items?limit=2
    {
      "data": [
        {"id": "itm_1001", "name": "Widget"},
        {"id": "itm_1002", "name": "Gadget"}
      ],
      "next_cursor": "eyJvIjoyfQ",
      "has_more": true
    }

    GET /v2/items?limit=2&cursor=eyJvIjoyfQ
    {
      "data": [
        {"id": "itm_1003", "name": "Gizmo"}
      ],
      "next_cursor": null,
      "has_more": false
    }

Things to call out in the docs:

1. Cursors are opaque. Clients must not decode, build or modify them.
2. A cursor is only valid with the same filters and sort order it was issued
   for. Changing `sort` while reusing a cursor returns 400 with the error
   code `cursor_mismatch`.
3. Cursors expire after 24 hours. An expired cursor returns 410 with the code
   `cursor_expired`, and the client should restart from the first page.
4. Inserting items while paginating does not cause duplicates or skipped rows
   for the default sort (`created_at` descending), because the cursor encodes
   the last seen position rather than an offset.
5. The deprecated `page` parameter still works until v3 but is ignored when
   `cursor` is present.

Example loop for the client libraries page (Python):

    def all_items(client, **filters):
        cursor = None
        while True:
            resp = client.get("/v2/items", params={**filters, "cursor": cursor, "limit": 100})
            yield from resp["data"]
            cursor = resp["next_cursor"]
            if not cursor:
                return

--- Comments ---

[comment 1] Reviewer: The loop sends `cursor=None` on the first request. Most HTTP
libraries drop None params, but requests-style clients in other languages might
send the string "null". Suggest building the params dict conditionally.

[comment 2] Author: Good point, updated the example to add the key only when a
cursor exists. Also added a note in the parameter table that `limit` above 200
is clamped silently rather than rejected.

[comment 3] Reviewer: Is the clamping really silent? I thought we return a
`X-Limit-Clamped: true` response header. Can you check the handler?

[comment 4] Author: Confirmed, the header exists. Added a sentence for it. I
also fixed the table so `has_more` is listed as boolean rather than string.

[comment 5] Reviewer: Looks good. Approving. Please run the docs linter before
merging, the code fence languages were missing in two places last time.

# Contributing: running the test suite

1. Create a virtual environment: `python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate`
2. Install dev dependencies: `pip install -e ".[dev]"`
3. Run the fast tests: `pytest -q -m "not slow"`
4. Run everything before opening a PR: `pytest -q`

## Writing tests

- Put tests in `tests/`, named `test_<module>.py`.
- Use fixtures from `conftest.py`; do not touch the network.
- Mark tests that take more than a second with `@pytest.mark.slow`.
- Prefer small parametrized tests over long ones with many asserts.

## Style

We use `ruff` for linting and `black` for formatting. Run `make fmt` before committing. The CI job fails if either tool reports a difference.

ISSUE #87: Crash with IndexError when the playlist has an odd number of tracks and shuffle is on

Opened by: user-reporter
Labels: bug, shuffle
Version: 2.3.1   OS: Linux   Python: 3.11.8

## What happens
Starting playback with shuffle enabled on a playlist of 7 tracks crashes on the
last track. With 8 tracks it works. Happens every time.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create a playlist with 7 files.
2. Run `tunebox play playlist.m3u --shuffle`
3. Let it play to the end.

## Output

    $ tunebox play playlist.m3u --shuffle
    [info] loaded 7 tracks
    [info] shuffle seed=18823
    [info] now playing 1/7
    [info] now playing 2/7
    [info] now playing 3/7
    [info] now playing 4/7
    [info] now playing 5/7
    [info] now playing 6/7
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "/usr/lib/python3.11/site-packages/tunebox/cli.py", line 112, in main
        player.run()
      File "/usr/lib/python3.11/site-packages/tunebox/player.py", line 74, in run
        self._advance()
      File "/usr/lib/python3.11/site-packages/tunebox/player.py", line 91, in _advance
        nxt = self.order[self.pos + 1]
    IndexError: list index out of range

## Expected
Playback stops cleanly after the last track, or loops if `--repeat` is given.

---- Comment by maintainer ----

Thanks, reproduced. The problem is in `_advance`. With shuffle on, `order` is
built by `_shuffle_pairs()`, which swaps tracks two at a time and drops the
final one when the length is odd, so `order` has 6 entries while `pos` runs up
to 6.

    def _shuffle_pairs(self, tracks, rng):
        order = []
        for i in range(0, len(tracks) - 1, 2):
            pair = [tracks[i], tracks[i + 1]]
            rng.shuffle(pair)
            order.extend(pair)
        return order          # last odd track is lost

That also explains why the log says "loaded 7 tracks" but only six are
played before the crash. I would replace the whole thing with a plain
`rng.sample(tracks, len(tracks))`; there was no good reason for the pairwise
approach.

---- Comment by contributor ----

Opened a pull request with that change plus a regression test:

    def test_shuffle_keeps_all_tracks():
        tracks = [f"t{i}" for i in range(7)]
        order = shuffled(tracks, random.Random(18823))
        assert sorted(order) == sorted(tracks)

    def test_last_track_ends_playback_cleanly(player):
        player.load(7)
        for _ in range(7):
            player.step()
        assert player.finished

This page explains the method. It contains no member data; the examples are made-up shapes of accounts, not real ones.

## Segment ideas to check each quarter

- Contractor-type accounts usually make up a large share of lapsed spend but a small share of lapsed members. Check this ratio each quarter and see whether it moves.
- Members who had a delivery issue in the last six months tend to churn faster. A simple comparison of churn rate with and without a logged delivery issue is enough.
- Financing customers usually lapse less, but a large balance on one item can change that.
- Points expiry complaints cluster in the weeks after a statement goes out.

## Typical offers, in order of cost

1. A small category discount on accessories.

- Do not mention returns history unless the member brings it up.
- Offer a callback time rather than pressing for a decision.

# Holiday season forecast and financing - sample retailer exercise

`docs/treasury/holiday_plan.md` - read by `forecast/seasonal.py`. This is the worked example for the retail finance module. "Sample Pantry Group" is fictional and every number is invented for teaching.

## Where the example quarter landed

Sample Pantry closed its example quarter with net sales of $2.00B (+2.0% comps) and diluted EPS of $0.40. In the case, last quarter's guidance was $0.50 to $0.60, so the quarter is a miss, driven by shrink ($40M above plan) and a poorly received app relaunch. The case asks students whether management should cut full-year guidance, and by how much. The example answer lowers it from $2.40-2.50 to $2.00-2.10.

## Financing in the case

- A finance committee approves a new $600M asset-based revolver, replacing a $450M facility that matures next year. Pricing in the example is SOFR plus 175 basis points, a typical range for such facilities.
- The case also plans a $250M senior notes add-on at 6.375%. Students compute the annual interest cost, which is $15.9M.
- Dividend: the example keeps the $0.30 quarterly dividend but removes the buyback. Students discuss why a company would favour dividends over repurchases when liquidity tightens.

## Acquisition in the case

The exercise has Sample Pantry buy "Fictional Grocers" (70 stores) for $520M, funded with the notes and cash. The target's EBITDA is $60M, so the multiple is 8.7x. The owners want a closing before year end for tax reasons, a common motive that the case notes. Students decide whether to present the deal with earnings or separately.

# Ember Tide: drop and matchmaking design (v0.9, pre-launch)

Working notes from the systems team for the Ashfall Games co-op title. Read
this before touching `loot/` or `queue/`; the numbers here are what the
live-ops tuning sheet is generated from, and the shipped client only sees the
outputs.

## Hidden Fortune meter

Every player carries a hidden "Fortune" value from 0 to 100. It is never
shown. The drop roller reads it on each kill and nudges the rare-tier odds so
that nobody goes dry for too long without us having to publish pity timers.

- Base rare chance: **3.2%** per elite kill, **0.6%** per trash kill.
- Fortune adds `0.045 * fortune` percentage points to the elite chance, so a
  player at 80 sees roughly 6.8%.
- Fortune rises by **+7** on an elite kill with no rare, resets to **12** on a
  rare drop. Boss kills never change it (this is deliberate, it keeps boss
  farming from being the optimal loop).
- Hard ceiling: if fortune reaches 94 the next elite kill is a guaranteed
  rare. We expect about 1 in 40 players to hit it in the first ten hours.

## Mercy seeds for returning players

Players who have been away 21+ days get fortune seeded to 55 for their first
three sessions. This is the retention lever the live-ops group wants kept
quiet; the community already suspects it and we neither confirm nor deny.

## Matchmaking: Skein rating

We do not use plain Elo. Internally the rating is called **Skein** and mixes
three signals:

| signal | weight |
|---|---|
| win/loss (team outcome) | 0.46 |
| revive-and-assist contribution per minute | 0.31 |
| survival share of the final objective | 0.23 |

Rating update uses K = 28 for the first 40 matches and K = 14 afterwards.
Parties of 3 are matched against solo-stacked lobbies only if the queue time
passes 95 seconds, and then the party is handicapped by -35 Skein per
additional member.

## Stealth difficulty

When a squad wipes twice on the same encounter, spawn density quietly drops
18% and enemy aggro range shrinks 10% for the next attempt. It restores over
three attempts. Analytics shows this converts about 70% of rage-quitters into
a clear without any visible "easy mode" prompt, which is the reason it stays
undocumented.

## Open items

- Test whether fortune seeding at 55 vs 65 changes day-30 retention (target
  readout: end of the closed beta in November).
- Anti-cheat team wants the Skein weights obfuscated in the client build.
- Decide whether to patent the stealth-difficulty curve; legal has a draft.

# Loot and matchmaking: how games commonly do it

Notes for the intro-to-game-design club at Ashfall Games' community open day.
Nothing here describes any shipped or unreleased title; the examples are
invented and the techniques are the ones discussed in public talks and
textbooks.

## Pity timers and hidden luck values

Many games track a hidden counter that makes rare drops more likely the longer
a player goes without one. This is often called a "pity timer" or "bad luck
protection", and several studios document theirs openly.

- Pick a base rare chance, for example **2%** per elite kill.
- Add a small bonus for every miss, say **+0.5** percentage points per dry
  kill, and reset the bonus when a rare drops.
- Set a hard ceiling (for example, guaranteed on the 60th kill) so players can
  always plan around the worst case.

Design question for the club: should the counter be visible? Visible timers
build trust, hidden ones keep the surprise. There is no single right answer.

## Welcome-back bonuses

Games often give lapsed players a small boost, such as double experience for a
weekend. Discuss what a studio would measure to find out whether it works:
return rate, session length, or something else.

## Matchmaking with Elo

The classic Elo update is public and short:

`new = old + K * (result - expected)`

where `expected = 1 / (1 + 10^((opponent - old) / 400))`. A common choice is
K = 32 for new players and a smaller K for veterans. A worked example with
made-up players: Mira (1500) beats Tobias (1600) with K = 32. Expected for Mira
is about 0.36, so she gains `32 * (1 - 0.36)` = roughly 20 points.

Team games complicate this. Some designs blend win/loss with a contribution
measure such as assists or objective time; the weights are a design choice and
every studio picks its own after testing.

## Dynamic difficulty

Dynamic difficulty adjustment means easing or tightening a game based on how
the player is doing. Published examples include rubber-banding in racing games
and adaptive enemy counts in shooters. Ethical questions to raise at the table:
should the game tell the player? Does hidden help feel like a gift or a
deception?

## Club exercises

- Sketch a pity timer for a fishing game and justify your numbers.
- Simulate 10,000 players with a 2% base chance and plot how many hit the
  ceiling.
- Write two sentences on whether an invisible difficulty drop is fair.

# Donor propensity model (Harvest v3)

Internal to the development team at Riverbend Relief.

## Why this exists

Our major-gift officers use the **Harvest** score to decide whom to call first. The model is the main reason our recurring-gift conversion rose from 4.1% to 6.8%, and other food banks keep asking how we do it. We do not publish it.

## Features

- Gift-gap regularity: standard deviation of days between gifts, bucketed in quarters
- `event_afterglow`: gifts within 21 days of a gala, weighted 2.4x
- Employer match eligibility (from the matching-gift vendor feed)
- Wealth-screen overlay: tier A/B only, never C

## Scoring

`score = 0.31*regularity + 0.27*afterglow + 0.22*match + 0.20*wealth`

Calls go to anyone above 0.58. Between 0.44 and 0.58 receives a mailed appeal. The cutoffs were chosen to keep the call list near 350 names a week.

## Handling

The weights file stays in the private repo; the vendor feed terms forbid sharing the derived scores.

# Route-time estimator: model card and tuning notes (Quarrystone Parcel)

Notes the last-mile data team keeps in the repo so the next person knows why
the estimator behaves as it does. It runs inside the driver app and sets every
"arriving between X and Y" window customers see. The accuracy (91.6% of
stops inside the promised 45-minute window) is a selling point to our
enterprise retailers, but the construction is ours alone.

## Stop-time model

`service_seconds = 38 + 11.5 * sqrt(parcels) + 52 * stairs_flag + 95 * signature_flag`

The square-root term fits the batching effect we measured on 180k stops in
2023: the second and third parcel add little, the eighth adds almost nothing.
Apartment buildings coded `MDU` with no concierge add a further 70 seconds per
floor above the third, which turned out to be our biggest single error source
before we added it.

## Traffic multiplier

We do not call a traffic API for the whole route. Instead each road segment
carries a learned hourly multiplier table (24 values, smoothed with a 0.35
exponential factor) built from our own GPS pings. The tables are the asset;
the mapping vendor never sees them. In the Eastport depot the 16:00-18:00
multiplier on the harbour ring road is 1.74, and we deliberately route around
it even when the vendor says it is clear.

## Buffer rule

The promised window is `[eta - 11 min, eta + 34 min]` for the first 30 stops
of a route, then widens by 40 seconds per stop after that. Customers always
see the window rounded to the nearest 5 minutes. Asymmetry is intentional: late
costs us roughly 3.2 times as much in credits as early costs in failed
delivery attempts.

## Driver-skill offset

A per-driver offset between -9% and +12% of service time is derived from the
trailing 60 days. It is never shown in the app and must not be referenced in
HR conversations; ops leadership signed this off on that basis.

## Open items

- Replace the sqrt batching term with a small gradient-boosted correction
  (prototype shaved 0.8 points off the late rate).
- Decide whether to file for protection on the asymmetric window rule. The
  patent attorney thinks the traffic-table update is the stronger claim.
- Retailers keep asking for the formula. The answer for now is no.

# Route-time estimator: tutorial notes (open-source delivery-sim course)

Notes that come with the toy last-mile simulator in the Quarrystone community
workshop repo. The estimator sets the "arriving between X and Y" windows in
the simulated driver app. It is a teaching model built from textbook ideas
and invented numbers, so participants can break it and rebuild it.

## Stop-time model

`service_seconds = 40 + 10 * sqrt(parcels) + 60 * stairs_flag + 90 * signature_flag`

The square-root shape is a common way to show diminishing returns when a
courier hands over several parcels at one door: the second and third parcel
add less than the first. Participants are invited to replace it with a
linear term and compare errors on the generated stops. Apartment buildings
are flagged `MDU` in the sample data and add a per-floor delay chosen only so
the example is visible in a chart.

## Traffic multiplier

The simulator uses a small invented table of 24 hourly multipliers. Values
sit between 1.0 and 1.6 with a morning and an evening peak, as in many public
traffic studies. Students smooth the table with an exponential factor (0.3 in
the starter code) and see how the factor changes the route time on a toy
map of a fictional town.

## Buffer rule

The promised window in the starter code is `[eta - 10 min, eta + 30 min]`,
rounded to the nearest 5 minutes. Exercise 4 asks why a window might be
asymmetric: what does it cost a carrier to arrive late versus early, and how
could you measure that? There is no right answer; bring examples from your own
experience as a customer.

## Driver variation

Real drivers differ in speed. The simulator draws a random offset for each
simulated driver between -10% and +10% of service time. Discussion: how
should a company use such data, and what are the fairness and privacy
concerns of measuring individuals? Please keep the discussion about the
simulation and not about any real employer.
